title: Debug: Product Search That Misuses Its API

description.summary: Debug a React product search page that misuses its search API, then add one small feature. Four user reports arrived: "The page says no products match before I type anything." "Typing a new query does not change the results." "When I type quickly, the results sometimes jump back to an older search." "When the search service is down, the page says Searching… forever." Find the root cause of each report in src/App.tsx, fix all four, and add the count line the product team asked for. Public interview reports describe this round at Walmart: an assessment section that asks candidates to debug a React or Angular app (2026), and a loop with a React debug session (2023). Concepts: react, debugging, effects, async, api-calls.

requirements: Work in `src/App.tsx`; treat `searchProducts` and the catalog as given.
Read the API response as it is typed: `{ items, total }`.
Search again whenever the query changes, starting with the empty query on mount.
Ignore a response that arrives after the query has changed again.
On a rejected request, replace the loading line with a readable `.status--error` line and keep the page usable for the next search.
Feature: on success, render `Showing X of Y products`, where Y is `total` from the API.
Keep the class names `.search`, `.status--loading`, `.result-row`, `.results` and `.empty`.
expectedBehavior: On first render the loading line is visible, then five `.result-row` items appear with `Showing 5 of 12 products`.
Typing `lamp` shows three rows and `Showing 3 of 3 products`.
Typing `l` and then `lamp` quickly ends with the three lamp rows, even after the slow `l` response arrives.
Typing `error` shows `Search failed: Search service unavailable` and no loading line; typing `desk` afterwards shows one row and no error.
A query without matches, such as `zzz`, shows `No products match "zzz".` with no rows and no count line.
implementationNotes: Replace the `any` in the `.then` callback with `SearchResponse`; TypeScript then points at the field the component reads.
Add `query` to the effect dependencies and set the loading state at the top of the effect.
Use a `cancelled` flag in the effect cleanup so only the latest request can update state.
Add a `.catch` that stores the error message; one status union keeps loading, error and success from overlapping.
techFocus: Typing API responses instead of any
A small feature on top of a fix

solutionBlock.overview:
Root causes, one per report:

1. The component reads `data.results`, but the API resolves `{ items, total }`; the `any` annotation hid the mismatch, so every search looked empty.
2. The effect has an empty dependency array, so it runs once and typing never searches again.
3. Nothing stops a slow response for an older query from overwriting newer results.
4. There is no `.catch`, so a rejection leaves `loading` true forever.

The fix keeps one `search` union (loading, success with `items` and `total`, error with a message), runs the request in an effect that depends on `[query]`, resets to loading at the top of the effect, flips a `cancelled` flag in the cleanup, and maps a rejection to the error state. The new count line reads `total` from the same success state.

**Test cases**
- Initial render shows five rows and `Showing 5 of 12 products`.
- `lamp` shows three rows; `l` then `lamp` still ends with three rows after the slow response.
- `error` shows the error line, and the next search clears it.
- `zzz` shows the empty state without rows or a count line.

approaches.title: Type the response, depend on the query, guard the request and catch the rejection
approaches.prose:
Start from the reports, not the code: each one maps to a single line.

1. Type the `.then` callback as `SearchResponse`. TypeScript immediately rejects `data.results`; read `data.items` and `data.total` instead.
2. Replace the parallel `results` and `loading` state with one `SearchState` union, so loading, success and error cannot overlap.
3. Depend on `[query]` and set `{ status: 'loading' }` at the top of the effect.
4. Declare `let cancelled = false`, return early in both handlers when it is set, and flip it in the cleanup. A slow `l` response now lands after its effect was cleaned up and is ignored.
5. Add `.catch` and store the message, so the error line replaces the loading line and the next search resets it.
6. Render the count line and rows only on success with `total > 0`, and the empty state only when a finished search returns `total === 0`.

pitfalls: Silencing the type error with `any` instead of typing the response, which is how `data.results` slipped in.
Adding `query` to the dependencies but not guarding the request, which trades the stale-results bug for a race.
Setting `loading` to false only in `.then`, so a rejection leaves the loading line on screen.
Showing the empty message whenever the list is empty, including while the first search is still loading.
Treating debounce as the fix for the race: it hides the race during fast typing, but a slow network still reorders responses.
techniques: Typing API responses at the boundary instead of using any.
useEffect with a cancelled flag in the cleanup.
A discriminated union for request state.
Reading every visible number from the latest successful response.

description.summary: Design and build a compound Select component: one API that works as a single-select or a multi-select and lets each option render custom content. The demo App already uses the API (Select, Select.Trigger, Select.Options and Select.Option); implement the four parts so the demo works. A public interview report of a Walmart Global Tech SDE 3 UI loop (January 2024) describes this prompt: design a dropdown API that can be single-select or multi-select and supports custom children, at the level of its high-level API; the candidate answered with compound components. This practice version makes that API runnable and checks it with behavior tests. Concepts: react, components, composition, context, accessibility.

requirements: Work in `src/App.tsx`. Keep the demo `App` as it is and implement `SelectRoot`, `SelectTrigger`, `SelectOptions` and `SelectOption`.
Share state between the parts through React context; the root owns the open state, and the value stays controlled through `value` and `onChange`.
Single mode: choosing an option calls `onChange(value)` and closes the list. Multi mode (`multiple`): choosing toggles the value in the array and keeps the list open.
The trigger is a button with `aria-haspopup="listbox"`, `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`; it shows the selected labels joined by commas, or the placeholder.
The list is a `role="listbox"` element that is `hidden` while closed and has `aria-multiselectable="true"` in multi mode.
Each option is `role="option"` with `aria-selected`; a `disabled` option has `aria-disabled="true"` and cannot be chosen.
Options render their children when given and their `label` otherwise; clicking anywhere inside an option chooses it.
Escape closes the open list.
expectedBehavior: Opening the fruit select and choosing Banana shows `Fruit: banana`, closes the list and puts Banana in the trigger.
Choosing Apple and then Dragon fruit leaves exactly one selected option.
Clicking Cherry, which is disabled, changes nothing and keeps the list open.
In the toppings select, Honey toggles on and Nuts toggles off while the list stays open.
The toppings trigger shows Nuts on first render, from the initial value, and `Nuts, Granola` after choosing Granola.
Escape closes the list and hides the listbox again.
implementationNotes: Type the props as a union of single and multi props so `value` and `onChange` match the mode at compile time.
Let options register their labels with the root, so the trigger can show labels for values chosen before the list was ever opened.
Keep the listbox mounted and toggle `hidden`, so registration works and `aria-controls` always points at a real element.

The preview passes `useState`, `useEffect`, `useMemo`, `useRef`, `useReducer`, `useContext`, `createContext` and `useCallback` in as globals; reach other hooks through `React`, for example `React.useLayoutEffect`.
techFocus: Controlled single and multi value APIs

solutionBlock.overview:
The root owns two pieces of state, `open` and a `labels` map, and derives `selected` from the controlled `value`: an array in multi mode, a zero- or one-item array in single mode. It provides one context with that state and three actions: `toggleOpen`, `choose` and `registerOption`.

`choose` toggles the value in multi mode and replaces it and closes the list in single mode. Each option registers its `label` in a layout effect, so the trigger can show `Nuts` before the list was ever opened. The listbox stays mounted and toggles `hidden`, which keeps registration working and `aria-controls` valid. A keydown handler on the root closes the list on Escape.

**Test cases**
- Banana closes the single list and appears in the trigger; Dragon fruit replaces Apple.
- Cherry is disabled and changes nothing.
- Toppings toggle while the list stays open, and the trigger lists their labels.
- A click on custom content inside an option chooses it.
- Escape closes the list.

approaches.title: Compound parts over one context, with option registration
approaches.prose:
1. Model the public API first: a union of single and multi props, and `Option` props with `value`, `label`, `disabled` and optional children.
2. In `SelectRoot`, keep `open` and a `labels` map in state and derive `selected` from `value`. Build the context value with `toggleOpen`, `choose` and `registerOption`, and render a visible label with an id for `aria-labelledby`.
3. `SelectTrigger` reads the context, joins the labels of the selected values or shows the placeholder, and sets `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`.
4. `SelectOptions` renders the listbox with `hidden={!open}` and `aria-multiselectable` in multi mode.
5. `SelectOption` registers its label in `React.useLayoutEffect`, sets `aria-selected` and `aria-disabled`, and calls `choose` on click unless it is disabled. A click on any child bubbles to the option.
6. A root `onKeyDown` closes the list on Escape. A `useSelectContext` helper throws a clear error when a part is rendered outside `Select`.

pitfalls: Typing `value` as `string | string[]` without the `multiple` discriminant, so callers can pass an array to a single select.
Copying the controlled value into internal state, which drifts from the parent after the first change.
Rendering the listbox only while open, so labels for initial values are unknown and the trigger shows raw values.
Registering options during render instead of in an effect, which writes state while React is rendering.
Closing the list after every choice in multi mode, which forces a reopen for each extra value.
techniques: Compound components that share one context.
Discriminated union props for single and multi modes.
Child registration through a stable callback and a layout effect.
The ARIA listbox pattern with aria-selected, aria-disabled and aria-multiselectable.

description.summary: Implement useMemo yourself, then build a context that serves API results to several components. Part 1: write useMemoized(factory, deps) without React's useMemo; it must return the cached value while the dependencies stay the same and recompute when one changes. Part 2: write UsersProvider and useUsers so three consumers share one request, see loading and error states, and reload together. A public interview report of a Walmart Global Tech Software Engineer 3 UI loop (November 2024) lists this exact sequence: implement useMemo, implement the Context API, then extend it to handle API results. Concepts: react, hooks, memoization, context, async.

requirements: Work in `src/App.tsx`. Keep the demo components (`App`, `UserSummary`, `UserList`, `UsersToolbar`) and the fake API as they are.

Part 1: implement `useMemoized(factory, deps)` without `useMemo`. Call `factory` on the first render, return the cached value while every dependency is the same by `Object.is`, and call `factory` again when a dependency or the number of dependencies changes.
Part 2: implement `UsersProvider` so it calls `fetchUsers()` once on mount, keeps a `UsersState` and provides `{ state, reload }` through `UsersContext`.
`reload` loads again: the state goes back to `loading`, then to `success` or `error`; a rejection becomes `{ status: 'error', message }`.
Ignore a response that arrives after a newer load started, and memoize the context value with `useMemoized`.
`useUsers()` returns the context value and throws a clear error outside `UsersProvider`.
expectedBehavior: The first render shows `Computed 1 time`; clicking Re-render twice keeps it at `Computed 1 time`.
Typing `an` shows Banana, Mango and Orange and `Computed 2 times`; another Re-render keeps it at 2.
After the first load, the summary shows `3 users`, the list shows three rows and the toolbar shows `Requests: 1`.
Reload shows `Loading users…`, then three rows and `Requests: 2`.
After Fail next request and Reload, the summary shows the error and no rows; the next Reload recovers with `Requests: 3`.
implementationNotes: Keep `{ deps, value }` in a `useRef`; compare dependencies in a small `sameDeps` helper.
Load in one `useEffect` inside the provider that depends on an `attempt` counter; `reload` bumps the counter.
Use a `cancelled` flag in the effect cleanup, and a `.catch` that stores the message.
Use `useCallback` for `reload` so the memoized context value stays stable between unrelated renders.

Loading, error and reload in one provider

solutionBlock.overview:
Part 1: keep `{ deps, value }` in a ref. On each render, compare the new dependencies with the cached ones by length and `Object.is`. If they differ, or nothing is cached yet, call the factory and store the result. Otherwise return the cached value. The factory runs during render, the same way React's own `useMemo` behaves.

Part 2: the provider owns the request. One effect depends on an `attempt` counter. It sets `loading`, calls `fetchUsers()` and maps the result to `success`, or a rejection to `error`. A `cancelled` flag drops responses from an older load. `reload` bumps the counter through a stable `useCallback`. The provider memoizes `{ state, reload }` with `useMemoized`, so unrelated renders keep the same context value. `useUsers` throws outside the provider.

**Test cases**
- Re-render keeps `Computed 1 time`; typing `an` recomputes once.
- Three consumers share one request: `Requests: 1`.
- Reload shows loading and ends with `Requests: 2`.
- A failed load shows the error; the next reload recovers.

approaches.title: A ref-backed memo hook and a provider that owns the request
approaches.prose:
1. `sameDeps(previous, next)` returns true only when both arrays have the same length and every pair is `Object.is` equal.
2. `useMemoized` keeps `{ deps, value }` in a `useRef`. On the first render, or when `sameDeps` fails, it calls the factory and stores the new pair. It always returns the cached value.
3. `UsersProvider` keeps `state` (a `UsersState` union) and an `attempt` counter. One `useEffect` with `[attempt]` sets `loading`, calls `fetchUsers()`, stores `success` or `error`, and flips `cancelled` in its cleanup.
4. `reload` is `useCallback(() => setAttempt((count) => count + 1), [])`. The context value is `useMemoized(() => ({ state, reload }), [state, reload])`.
5. `useUsers` reads the context and throws `useUsers must be used inside <UsersProvider>` when it is missing.

pitfalls: Comparing dependencies with `===`, so a NaN dependency recomputes on every render.
Storing the memoized value in state, which triggers an extra render every time it refreshes.
Fetching inside `useUsers`, so every consumer starts its own request.
Recreating `{ state, reload }` on every provider render, which re-renders every consumer even when nothing changed.
Forgetting the `.catch`, which leaves every consumer on the loading state after a rejection.
techniques: Ref-based caching with dependency comparison.
Object.is equality, the rule React uses for dependencies.
A provider that owns one request for many consumers.
A retry counter in the effect dependencies.

description.summary: Build a planner for an industrial battery site: the user picks how many of four battery sizes to install, the planner adds transformers automatically, totals the budget, net energy and land size, and lays the devices out in rows that never exceed 100 ft. Public repositories show this take-home at Tesla Energy: a candidate published the UI evaluation brief, and at least 22 independent repositories build it between 2023 and 2026. This practice version is modelled on that reported take-home, with our own device catalog and wording, and fixes the layout rule so the tests can check it. Concepts: react, state, forms, algorithms, layout.

requirements: Work in `src/App.tsx`; keep `BATTERIES`, `TRANSFORMER` and the constants as given.

A valid quantity is a whole number from 0 to `MAX_QUANTITY` (50). An invalid one counts as 0 and shows `

Use a whole number from 0 to 50.

`.
Add one transformer for every two batteries, rounded up, and show `Transformers: N`.
Show the budget as `$` with thousands separators, the net energy in MWh (transformers subtract energy), and the land as `W ft × D ft`.
Pack the devices into rows: largest first, each device into the first row that still has room, never wider than `SITE_WIDTH_FT` (100 ft).
Render one `.layout-row` per row with `data-width` set to its width in feet, and one `.layout-device` per device with `data-device` set to its id.
The land is the widest row times the number of rows times `ROW_DEPTH_FT` (10 ft). Reset sets every quantity back to 0.
expectedBehavior: With nothing chosen the budget is `$0`, the net energy `0 MWh` and the layout is empty.
One Battery XL gives `$134,000`, `3.95 MWh`, `Transformers: 1` and `50 ft × 10 ft`.
Three Battery XL give two rows of 100 ft and 40 ft and `100 ft × 20 ft`.
Twelve Battery S give six transformers, rows of 100 ft and 80 ft, `$198,000` and `10.5 MWh`.
An invalid quantity such as `-1` or `1.5` shows the error and does not change the totals.
Reset returns every quantity to 0 and empties the layout.
implementationNotes: Keep the raw input strings in state and derive everything else in one `useMemo`; never store totals in state.
Write the rules as small pure functions (`parseQuantity`, `transformersFor`, `packRows`) so they are easy to test and explain.
`BATTERIES` is listed smallest first, so pack from a copy sorted largest first; placing each device into the first row with room is first-fit decreasing.
Extensions such as saving and resuming a plan, or an export, are discussed in the follow-ups and are not checked.
techFocus: Derived state from raw form input

solutionBlock.overview:
Keep only the raw quantity strings in state. One `useMemo` derives the rest:

1. Validate each quantity with `parseQuantity`: a whole number from 0 to 50, or `null`. Invalid ones count as 0, and the planner shows one error line.
2. Expand the counts into a device list and add `transformersFor(batteries)` transformers, which is `Math.ceil(batteries / 2)`.
3. Sum the cost and the net energy; transformers subtract 0.25 MWh each.
4. `packRows` sorts a copy largest first and puts each device into the first row with room, starting a new row when none fits. The land is the widest row times rows × 10 ft.

Rows render with `data-width`, so the 100 ft rule is visible to the tests and to a reviewer.

**Test cases**
- Zero state, then one Battery XL: `$134,000`, `3.95 MWh`, one transformer, `50 ft × 10 ft`.
- 3 batteries need 2 transformers; 4 batteries still need 2.
- Three Battery XL pack into rows of 100 ft and 40 ft.
- Twelve Battery S and six transformers pack into rows of 100 ft and 80 ft.
- One Battery L and two Battery XL pack into rows of 100 ft and 30 ft; packing in catalog order would give 90 ft and 40 ft.
- Invalid input shows the error; Reset clears everything.

approaches.title: Raw input in state, pure rules, one derived site object
approaches.prose:
1. `parseQuantity(raw)` trims, accepts only digits, and caps the value at `MAX_QUANTITY`; anything else returns `null`.
2. `transformersFor(count)` returns `Math.ceil(count / 2)`.
3. `packRows(devices)` copies and sorts by width descending, then for each device finds the first row whose width plus the device still fits in 100 ft, or opens a new row.
4. In `App`, a `useMemo` over `quantities` builds the device list, adds the transformers, sums cost and energy, packs the rows, and computes width and depth.
5. The JSX renders the inputs, the error line when any quantity is invalid, the summary with formatted values, and the rows with `data-width` and one block per device. Reset writes `EMPTY_QUANTITIES` back to state.

pitfalls: Storing totals or rows in state next to the quantities, so they drift when one update is missed.
Rounding transformers down: three batteries need two transformers, not one.
Packing in catalog order: one Battery L and two Battery XL then need rows of 90 ft and 40 ft instead of 100 ft and 30 ft.
Parsing input with `parseInt`, which turns `1.5` into 1 and `-1` into a negative count.
Summing decimals without formatting, so `3.9500000000000006 MWh` reaches the screen.
techniques: Derived state with a single useMemo.
Pure helper functions for business rules.
First-fit decreasing bin packing.
Intl-based money formatting with toLocaleString.

title: File Explorer Tree with Keyboard Navigation

description.summary: Build a file explorer that renders a nested folder tree from data, sorted with folders first, where folders open and close and files can be selected. Then make it a real tree widget: ARIA tree roles and states, one tab stop that follows focus, and arrow-key navigation that opens folders, enters them and climbs back to the parent. An empty folder is still a folder, and Collapse all must never strand the tab stop inside a closed folder. Concepts: recursion, accessibility, keyboard navigation, state management.

requirements: Work in `src/App.tsx`. Keep `FILES` and the `FileNode` type as they are; a node with a `children` array is a folder, even when the array is empty.
Render the tree with `role="tree"` on the list and `role="treeitem"` on every node, with `aria-level` and a `data-path` holding the slash-separated path, for example `src/components/Button.tsx`.
Sort every level: folders first, then files, both by name ignoring case.

Folders start closed. Clicking a folder's `.row` toggles it and its `aria-expanded`; an open folder renders its children inside `role="group"`, and an empty one shows `Empty folder` in an element with the class `empty`. Files have no `aria-expanded`.
Clicking a file's `.row` selects it: that file gets `aria-selected="true"`, every other file `aria-selected="false"`, and `.selection` shows `Selected: <path>`.

Exactly one treeitem has `tabIndex` 0 and it follows focus. ArrowDown, ArrowUp, Home and End move focus through the visible items; ArrowRight opens a closed folder or moves into an open one; ArrowLeft closes an open folder or moves to the parent; Enter toggles a folder or selects a file.
Collapse all closes every folder; if the active item disappears, its nearest visible ancestor takes the tab stop.
expectedBehavior: The first level reads `public`, `src`, `package.json`, `README.md`.
Opening `src` shows `components`, `styles`, `App.tsx`, `index.tsx`.
Opening `src/styles` shows `Empty folder`.
Selecting `src/components/Button.tsx` and then `package.json` leaves only `package.json` selected.
From `public`, ArrowDown focuses `src`, End focuses `README.md`, Home returns to `public`.
After Collapse all with `src/components/Tree.tsx` active, `src` holds the only `tabIndex` 0.
implementationNotes: Keep the open folders in a `Set` of ids and derive a flat list of visible items for keyboard movement.
Put one `onKeyDown` on the tree and read the item from `event.target.closest('[role="treeitem"]')`.
Keep element refs in a `Map` and call `focus()` when the tab stop moves.
Derive the tab stop during render: the active item if it is visible, otherwise its nearest visible ancestor.
techFocus: ARIA tree view roles and states
Keyboard navigation over a visible-items list

solutionBlock.overview:
Keep three pieces of state: the set of open folder ids, the selected file path and the active item id. Derive everything else during render. A recursive `renderNodes` sorts each level, writes the ARIA roles and states, and renders children only for open folders. A flat `visible` list of what is on screen powers the keyboard: ArrowDown and ArrowUp step through it, Home and End jump to its ends, ArrowRight opens a folder and then enters it, and ArrowLeft closes it and then climbs to the parent. The tab stop is derived too: the active item when it is visible, otherwise its nearest visible ancestor, so Collapse all can never hide it.

**Test cases**
- Folders first, then files, ignoring case.
- Toggling `src` and an empty `src/styles`.
- One selected file at a time.
- Arrow keys, Home and End with one tab stop.
- Right and Left arrows, Enter, and Collapse all keeping a visible tab stop.

approaches.title: Recursive render, flat visible list and a derived tab stop
approaches.prose:
1. `isFolder` checks for a `children` array, and `sortNodes` puts folders first and compares names with `localeCompare` and `sensitivity: 'base'`.
2. `visibleItems` flattens the sorted tree, descending only into open folders, and records each item's path, level and parent.
3. `tabStopId` walks from the active id up `PARENT_OF` until it finds a visible item.
4. `focusItem` sets the active id and focuses the element from the ref map.
5. One `onKeyDown` on the tree maps ArrowDown, ArrowUp, Home, End, ArrowRight, ArrowLeft and Enter onto the visible list and calls `preventDefault` for the keys it handles.
6. `renderNodes` writes `role`, `aria-level`, `aria-expanded` on folders, `aria-selected` on files and `tabIndex`, and renders `role="group"` only for open folders.

pitfalls: Treating a folder with an empty children array as a file.
Sorting with plain string comparison, which puts README.md above package.json.
Putting the click handler on the list item, so a click on a file also toggles every ancestor folder.
Keeping the tab stop on an item that a collapse removed, so Tab skips the whole tree.
Setting aria-expanded on files, which screen readers announce as collapsed folders.
techniques: Recursive rendering with a derived flat list for navigation.
Roving tabindex with element refs.
Deriving focus state during render instead of syncing it in handlers.

title: Build a Dropdown as a JavaScript Class, Then Port It to React

description.summary: Build one basemap picker twice: first as a plain JavaScript class that creates and updates its own DOM, then as a React component. Both versions share a pure reducer, render the same combobox and listbox markup, work with the mouse and the keyboard, close on Escape and on outside clicks, and report a change only when the selection changes. The checks run the same cases against both versions, so the port is tested against the original. Concepts: dom, classes, react. React focus: moving imperative DOM updates into state, sharing a reducer through useReducer, refs for focus, and effect cleanup.

requirements: Work in `src/App.tsx`. Keep `VanillaBasemapPicker`, `Status` and `App` as given, and implement `pickerReducer`, the `BasemapPicker` class and `ReactBasemapPicker`.
Make `pickerReducer` pure and use it in both versions: no DOM, no React and no callbacks inside it, and the same state object back when an action changes nothing.

Render the same DOM in both versions: a `.picker` root, a `.picker-label` span with the id `<idPrefix>-label`, a `button.picker-trigger` with `role="combobox"`, `aria-haspopup="listbox"`, `aria-controls`, `aria-labelledby` and `aria-expanded`, and a `ul.picker-list` with `role="listbox"` and the id `<idPrefix>-list` that stays mounted and is `hidden` while closed.
Render each option as `li.picker-option` with `role="option"`, the id `<idPrefix>-opt-<index>` and `aria-selected`. The trigger text is the selected label.
Clicking the trigger opens or closes the list. Clicking an option selects it, closes the list and moves focus back to the trigger.

Handle keys on the trigger: ArrowDown and ArrowUp open a closed list on the selected option; in an open list they move the active option and stop at the ends, Home and End jump to the first and last option, Enter selects the active option and Escape closes without selecting.
Mark the active option with the class `is-active` and point the trigger at it with `aria-activedescendant` while the list is open; remove the attribute when the list closes.
Close the list on a click outside the picker by listening on `document`. Remove that listener in `destroy()` and in the React effect cleanup.
Call `onChange(item)` only when the selection changes. Choosing the selected option again reports nothing.
Render labels as text. The last option is a user-named preset whose name contains angle brackets.
expectedBehavior: On first render both triggers show Satellite, both lists are hidden and both status lines report 0 changes.
Choosing Streets with the mouse updates that version's trigger and status line to 1 change and puts focus back on its trigger; choosing Streets again keeps the count at 1.
ArrowDown opens the list on Satellite, End jumps to the preset, Home returns to Satellite, and two more ArrowDown presses followed by Enter select Streets with focus still on the trigger.
Escape, or a click on the panel heading, closes the list and keeps Satellite selected.
The preset appears as `My preset <draft>` in the list, in the trigger and in the status line.
A choice in one version never changes the other.
After the preview unmounts, no listener remains on `document`.
implementationNotes: Create the class's elements once in the constructor and update their text and attributes in `render()`. Rebuilding them on every render loses focus, and the document listener then receives a click target that is no longer in the DOM.
Handle option clicks with one listener on the list: find the option with `closest('[role="option"]')` and read its index from a `data-index` attribute.
Store the handlers as arrow-function fields, so `removeEventListener` receives the same function that `addEventListener` did.

In React, take the state from `useReducer(pickerReducer, …)`. In event handlers, run the same reducer on the current state to decide whether to call `onChange`, instead of watching the selection in an effect that also fires on mount.
Call `preventDefault()` only for the keys the picker handles, so the page does not scroll. Enter and Space on a closed trigger already click the button.
The preview passes `useState`, `useEffect`, `useMemo`, `useRef`, `useReducer`, `useContext`, `createContext` and `useCallback` in as globals; reach any other hook through `React`.
techFocus: Plain JavaScript DOM components with classes
One pure reducer shared by two renderers
Porting imperative DOM updates to React state
Combobox and listbox ARIA with aria-activedescendant
Listener cleanup on destroy and unmount

solutionBlock.overview:
Put every state change in one pure `pickerReducer` over `{ open, activeIndex, selectedIndex, count }`. Both versions send it the same actions, `toggle`, `close`, `choose` and `key`, and it returns the same object when nothing changes, so each version can skip rendering and side effects.

The class builds its label, trigger, list and options once and attaches four listeners. Its `send(action)` method runs the reducer, calls `render()` and fires `onChange` only when `selectedIndex` moved. `render()` updates text and attributes in place, so the focused trigger survives every update, and `destroy()` removes all four listeners, including the one on `document`.

The React component keeps the same contract. `useReducer(pickerReducer, …)` holds the state, JSX replaces `render()`, an `onClick` per option replaces the delegated listener, and an effect with a cleanup replaces the constructor and `destroy()` pair for the document listener. Event handlers run the same reducer on the current state to decide whether to report a change, which keeps `onChange` out of the reducer and out of an effect.

**Test cases**
- Both versions render closed with Satellite selected and toggle on trigger clicks.
- A mouse choice updates the trigger, reports one change, keeps the count when the same option is chosen again and returns focus to the trigger.
- Arrow keys, Home and End move the active option and stop at the ends, and Enter selects it.
- Escape and an outside click close the list without changing the selection.
- The preset label renders as text.
- Unmounting leaves no listener on document.
- A choice in one version does not change the other.

approaches.title: One pure reducer, rendered by a class and by a component
approaches.prose:
Write the reducer first and check it against the keyboard table: on a closed list, ArrowDown and ArrowUp open on the selected option; on an open list they move and stop at the ends, Home and End jump, Enter selects the active option, and Escape and Tab close. A `handlesKey` helper names the keys whose default action the picker prevents.

Then the class:

1. In the constructor, create the label, the trigger button, the list and one `li` per option, set the attributes that never change, write labels with `textContent` and append everything to the host.
2. Add four listeners: click and keydown on the trigger, one delegated click on the list, and click on `document` for outside clicks.
3. `send(action)` keeps the previous state, runs the reducer, returns early when the object did not change, renders, and calls `onChange` when `selectedIndex` moved.
4. `render()` writes the trigger text, `aria-expanded`, `aria-activedescendant`, the list's `hidden` flag and each option's `aria-selected` and `is-active` class onto the existing nodes.
5. `destroy()` removes the four listeners and the root.

Then the port. `useReducer` replaces the state field, JSX replaces `render()`, an `onClick` per option replaces the delegated listener, and `useRef` provides the root for the outside-click test and the trigger for focus. One `useEffect` adds the document listener and returns its removal; because `dispatch` is stable, that listener never reads stale state. `send` runs the reducer on the current state to see whether the selection changes, then dispatches and calls `onChange` from the event handler.

pitfalls: Rebuilding the class markup with `innerHTML` on every render: labels with `<` turn into elements, focus drops and the outside-click listener sees a detached target.
Adding listeners with inline arrow functions and removing new ones in `destroy()`, so nothing is removed.
Reporting changes from a `useEffect` that watches the selection, which also fires on mount and reports a change nobody made.
Rendering the React list only while it is open, so `aria-controls` points at nothing and the markup no longer matches the class.
Keeping picker state in a module-level variable, so the two pickers on the page change together.
Copying the transitions into the React component instead of reusing the reducer, so the two versions drift apart.
techniques: A pure reducer shared by an imperative and a declarative renderer.
Event delegation with `closest()` and data attributes.
Arrow-function class fields for removable listeners.
Combobox and listbox ARIA with `aria-activedescendant`.
Effect cleanup for listeners on document.

premiumPreview.summary: Debug a dubbing review player whose transcript highlight lags behind the audio, then add a position line. Each of four reviewer reports points to a different mistake in how the component runs its clock, filters its lines and loads a transcript.
learningOutcomes: Trace a control that does nothing back to a stale closure in an interval callback.
Stop a timer with an effect cleanup instead of a flag.
Replace an effect that syncs state with a value derived during render.
Keep a late response for an old selection from overwriting a newer one.

solutionBlock.overview:
Root causes, one per report:

1. The clock effect depends on `[playing]` only, so its interval callback keeps the rate it captured when playback started; 2× changes the state and nothing else.
2. The same effect returns no cleanup, so Pause leaves the old interval running and the next Play adds a second one.
3. The filter lives in an effect that depends on `[lines]`, so typing never reruns it.
4. The transcript effect applies whichever response arrives, so the slow Spanish transcript replaces the English one that was already on screen.

The fix lists `rate` and the line count as dependencies of the clock effect, clears the interval in its cleanup, clamps the position at the end and stops playing there; derives the filtered lines with `useMemo` over the lines and the query; and flips a `cancelled` flag in the transcript effect cleanup so only the latest request can set the lines. The new position line reads the same active index as the highlight.

**Test cases**
- The English transcript loads with its first line highlighted.
- `mix` leaves three lines at once.
- Play, Pause: the time stays at `2.0 s`.
- 2× reaches `Finished` in half the time.
- Spanish then English keeps English on screen after the slow response.
- The position line reads `Line 3 of 8` after a second of playing.

approaches.title: Clean up the clock, derive the filter and guard the transcript request
approaches.prose:
Start from the reports, not the code: each one maps to one line.

1. Give the clock effect the dependencies it reads, `[playing, rate, total]`, and return a cleanup that clears the interval. A rate change now restarts the timer with the new rate, Pause clears it, and a second Play cannot stack a second timer.
2. Clamp the position in the updater, `Math.min(current + rate, total)`, derive `finished` from it, and stop playing when it is reached; the cleanup does the rest.
3. Delete the filter effect and its state. `useMemo` over `[lines, query]` returns the filtered lines in the same render as the keystroke.
4. Declare `let cancelled = false` in the transcript effect, return early in the `.then` when it is set, and flip it in the cleanup. The slow Spanish response now lands after the user left Spanish and is ignored.
5. Render `Line {activeIndex + 1} of {total}` from the same `activeIndex` the highlight uses.

Say what each edit does as you make it: the interviewer is listening for the cause (a captured value, a missing cleanup, an effect that syncs state, an unguarded response), not for the symptom.

title: Downloadable Files Table: Select All Across Pages

description.summary: Build a table of downloadable files from a sensor export with a filter, a sort and a select all that stays correct across pages. A public 2025 interview account describes a CrowdStrike take-home of this shape: a table with a few rows of downloadable files and their details, built from a screenshot, then a review with two engineers on filtering and sorting, thousands of entries and what happens when someone selects all, moves to another page and deselects a few. This is a FrontendAtlas practice version, not the company's brief. Concepts: react, state management, pagination, tables, accessibility.

requirements: Work in `src/App.tsx`; treat `FILES` and `PAGE_SIZE` as given.
Filter the rows by a case-insensitive name match and sort them by name or by size; a filter change returns to page one.

Store the selection as a mode plus exceptions keyed by file id, so select all covers every matching available file on every page without listing ids, and a row unticked on another page stays unticked.

The header checkbox is checked when every matching available file is selected, mixed (`aria-checked="mixed"` and the `indeterminate` property) when some are, and unchecked when none are; checking it from the mixed state selects all.
Unavailable files show `Not available yet` and cannot be selected.
Show `N selected` in `.selection-count`, enable `.download` only with a selection, show an `.empty` line when nothing matches, and clear the selection when the filter changes.

Keep the class names `.row`, `.row--selected`, `.name`, `.size`, `.status--unavailable`, `.select-all`, `.select-row`, `.filter`, `.sort-name`, `.sort-size`, `.prev`, `.next`, `.page`, `.selection-count`, `.download` and `.empty`.
expectedBehavior: The first page shows eight rows sorted by name, starting with `agent-config-2026-10.json`, and `Page 1 of 3`.
Select all reads `22 selected`; page two shows seven ticked rows and one unavailable file whose checkbox is disabled.
Unticking a row on page two reads `21 selected` and turns the header mixed; page one still shows eight ticked rows.
Filtering by `report` leaves six rows on one page, and select all then reads `6 selected`.
Sort by size puts `api-keys-rotation.log` (8 KB) first; Sort by name restores the name order.
A filter with no match shows `No files match` and disables Download.
implementationNotes: Hold `{ mode: 'none' | 'all', exceptions: Set<string> }`; a file is selected when it is available and its id is in the exceptions for mode none, or missing from them for mode all.
Derive the matching rows with `useMemo` over the filter and the sort, then slice the current page.
Count the selected files among the matching available ones, and derive the header state from that count.
Set the header checkbox `indeterminate` property in an effect; React cannot set it from markup.

Derived state for filtering, sorting and paging
Mixed checkbox state and its accessibility

premiumPreview.summary: Build a downloadable-files table whose select all stays correct across pages, filters and sorts. The selection model is the part a take-home review probes: a mode plus exceptions keyed by file id.
learningOutcomes: Model the selection as a mode plus exceptions so select all never lists ids.
Keep a row unticked on another page unticked, with a mixed header.
Derive filtered, sorted and paged rows without copying them into state.
Keep unavailable files out of every selection and count.

solutionBlock.overview:
The selection is the whole exercise. Store it as `{ mode, exceptions }` keyed by file id: select all sets the mode to all with no exceptions, a tick or an untick toggles one id in the exceptions, and a file counts as selected when it is available and the mode and the exceptions agree. Paging, filtering and sorting are a slice of one derived list, so none of them can move or lose a tick.

The header state comes from counts over the matching available files: all, none or mixed. Mixed sets `aria-checked="mixed"` in markup and the `indeterminate` property in an effect, because React cannot render that property. A filter change clears the selection and returns to page one, so a hidden file never reaches the download; say that decision out loud in the review.

**Test cases**
- The first page shows eight rows sorted by name.
- Select all reads `22 selected` and page two shows seven ticked rows.
- An untick on page two reads `21 selected`, turns the header mixed and leaves page one ticked.
- A filter narrows to six rows and select all follows it.
- Sort by size puts the smallest file first.
- A filter with no match shows an empty line and disables Download.

approaches.title: Mode plus exceptions over one derived list
approaches.prose:
Build it in the order a reviewer will question it.

1. Derive `matching` with `useMemo` over the filter and the sort, compute the page count, clamp the page, and slice the visible rows.
2. Hold the selection as `{ mode: 'none' | 'all', exceptions: Set<string> }`. A file is selected when it is available and either the mode is all and its id is not an exception, or the mode is none and its id is.
3. Count the selected files among the matching available ones, and derive the header state from that count; set `indeterminate` in an effect and `aria-checked="mixed"` in markup.
4. Select all from none or mixed sets the mode to all; from all it clears. A row toggles its own id in the exceptions.
5. A filter change clears the selection and returns to page one; the download button reads the same count.

In the review, the same model answers the follow-ups: thousands of rows change nothing, because the selection never listed ids, and the download request sends the mode and the exceptions.

title: Listing Booking Widget: Dates, Guests and Total Price

description.summary: Build a booking widget for one listing: it prices a stay from check-in and check-out dates and the number of adults and children, greys out Book now when the dates are booked, and confirms in an accessible dialog. A curated 2025 account describes an Airbnb full-stack phone screen of this shape: 40 minutes of live coding on a small booking widget, then 20 minutes of product discussion. This is a FrontendAtlas practice version, not the company's prompt. Concepts: react, forms, derived state, dates, dialogs, accessibility.

requirements: Work in `src/App.tsx`; treat `LISTING` and `RATES` as given.
From the two date inputs, count the nights and show the nightly line (`$180 x 3 nights`) with its amount, the cleaning fee and the total; without both dates there is no total.

The nightly price covers two guests; each guest after that, adult or child, adds `$25` a night. Adults start at one and never go below it, children start at zero, and both plus buttons are disabled at four guests.

A check-out on or before check-in shows `Check-out must be after check-in`; a stay that overlaps a range in `LISTING.booked` shows `Those dates are booked`. In both cases there is no total and Book now is disabled.

Book now opens a dialog with `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal="true"` and a title, summarizing the dates, nights, guests and total; focus moves to Confirm booking, and Escape or Cancel closes it and returns focus to Book now.
Confirm booking closes the dialog, shows `Booked: Lakeside cabin, Dec 10 to Dec 13` and disables Book now.

Keep the class names `.check-in`, `.check-out`, `.adults-minus`, `.adults-plus`, `.adults-count`, `.children-minus`, `.children-plus`, `.children-count`, `.price-line`, `.price-amount`, `.cleaning-fee`, `.total`, `.date-error`, `.availability`, `.book`, `.confirm-dialog`, `.confirm-summary`, `.confirm`, `.cancel` and `.booked-message`.
expectedBehavior: Book now is disabled until both dates are picked.
December 10 to 13 for one adult reads `$180 x 3 nights`, `$540`, a `$60` cleaning fee and a `$600` total.
Three adults and one child read `$230 x 3 nights` and a `$750` total, and both plus buttons are disabled.
December 23 to 26 reads `Those dates are booked`; December 27 to 29 is free and totals `$420`.
The dialog reads `Dec 10 to Dec 13 · 3 nights · 1 guest · $600` with focus on Confirm booking.
Escape closes the dialog and focus returns to Book now.
implementationNotes: Derive one quote with `useMemo` over the dates and the guest count: empty, invalid, booked or ready with the nights and amounts.
Count nights as whole UTC days: parse the ISO date parts with `Date.UTC` and subtract.
Treat booked ranges as half-open: a stay overlaps when it starts before the range ends and ends after it starts.
Format amounts with `Intl.NumberFormat` in the listing currency with no fraction digits, and move focus with refs in an effect.
techFocus: Derived state for a price breakdown
Date arithmetic without time zone drift
Product follow-ups: currencies and request counts

premiumPreview.summary: Build a listing booking widget that prices a stay from two dates and a guest count, greys out Book now on booked dates and confirms in an accessible dialog. The review signal is one derived quote that every line and the button read.
learningOutcomes: Derive the nights, the price lines and the total from one quote.
Count nights in UTC days and check booked dates as half-open ranges.

Confirm in a dialog that takes focus, closes on Escape and returns focus.

solutionBlock.overview:
Everything on the widget reads one quote derived from the two dates and the guest count. The quote is empty until both dates exist, invalid when check-out is not after check-in, booked when the stay overlaps a booking, and otherwise ready with the nights, the nightly price, the stay and the total. The lines, the total and Book now all read it, so they can never disagree.

Nights are whole UTC days, so a clock change cannot turn three nights into 2.96, and booked ranges are half-open, so a check-out on the morning a booking starts is fine. The confirmation is a dialog that takes focus, closes on Escape or Cancel and returns focus to Book now.

**Test cases**
- Book now is disabled until both dates are picked.
- Three nights for one adult total $600.
- Four guests pay $230 a night and the plus buttons disable.
- A check-out before check-in shows an error and no total.
- An overlap with a booking greys out Book now; a stay that starts on the booking's last morning is free.
- The dialog takes focus, closes on Escape and returns focus.
- Confirm shows the booked message.

approaches.title: One derived quote, half-open ranges and a focused dialog
approaches.prose:
Build it in the order the interviewer will follow up.

1. Derive `quote` with `useMemo` over the dates and `adults + children`: empty without both dates, invalid when the nights are not positive, booked when a range overlaps, else ready.
2. Count nights with a `toDay` helper over `Date.UTC`, and compare ISO strings for the overlap: `checkIn < range.to && range.from < checkOut`.
3. Put the extra guest fee in the nightly price, and give both counters one cap: `guests < LISTING.maxGuests`.
4. Enable Book now only for a ready quote, and show the reason when it is not: the date error or the booked message.
5. Open the dialog, move focus to Confirm booking in an effect, close on Escape or Cancel and return focus to Book now.

In the product follow-ups, the same quote answers most questions: a currency picker changes one formatter and converts the rounded nightly price once, so the lines still add up; fewer requests come from fetching a month of availability at a time and pricing on the client; an offline cache keeps the last availability with the time it was fetched and says so; and payment details never go into that cache.
